retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path
the XOR is applied to an unrelated buffer, not the input being checked
misfire_risks: the key may be position-dependent / rolling rather than a single constant byte; assuming a single-byte key yields a wrong pre-image -- verify the key schedule before inverting
minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

retrieved_cards.title: Disassembly can desync and show a plausible-but-wrong instruction stream
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Instructions are being read at a fixed alignment where the real code overlaps, jumps into the middle of an instruction, or uses anti-disassembly, so the decoded stream may not be what executes.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A byte stream has multiple decodings; a linear or fixed-offset decode can lock onto the wrong one, producing instructions that look real but are not executed as shown.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Follow control flow into the region to fix the instruction boundaries, and re-disassemble at that alignment; where two decodings are possible, the one an incoming edge lands on is the one that runs.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The disassembly listing is the executed code, so I can reverse it as-is.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Verify the decode alignment against control flow; re-disassemble from the real entry points and follow the jumps to recover the instructions that actually run.
not_applicable_when: the disassembly alignment is confirmed by an incoming control-flow edge
the code region is known-clean with no overlap/anti-disasm
misfire_risks: most disassembly is correctly aligned; suspect desync specifically around indirect jumps, inline data, or obfuscated regions, not everywhere
minimum_evidence_before_use: a region shows overlap / jump-into-instruction / anti-disassembly characteristics
its alignment has not been confirmed against an incoming control-flow edge

retrieved_cards.title: Inline data or junk bytes can be rendered as instructions
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Bytes that are actually data (jump tables, constants, padding) or deliberate junk are being decoded and read as executable instructions.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: The boundary between code and data is ambiguous to the tool; non-code bytes decoded as instructions create spurious logic that never executes.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Check how the region is referenced (branched to, vs loaded as data) and whether any control-flow edge reaches it; a region with only data references is not code.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: These decoded instructions are real code, so they participate in the logic.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Confirm a control-flow edge reaches the region as code, rather than it being referenced as data, before reversing it.
not_applicable_when: the region is confirmed to be the target of a control-flow edge
the bytes are clearly referenced as data
misfire_risks: genuine code can look data-like; base the call on references and reachability, not on the bytes looking unusual
minimum_evidence_before_use: a region decoded as instructions has data-like or junk characteristics
no control-flow edge into it has been identified

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract data-as-code artifact; no task specifics. Distinct from desync (alignment of real code).

retrieved_cards.title: A candidate never traced to a decision that would accept it
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A candidate has been adopted, but no comparison in the binary has been identified whose outcome on that candidate selects the accepting branch; the analysis proceeds as though it had passed.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Absence of an observed contradiction is conflated with positive support. With no execution available a candidate carries no acceptance evidence at all until it is traced to the comparison that decides.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Name the deciding comparison and both of its operands. If either operand cannot be pinned to a concrete value, the candidate is unsupported rather than confirmed -- that is a different state from being wrong, and it should be said explicitly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Nothing in the analysis contradicted this candidate, so it is the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Acceptance has to be positively derived: name the comparison that decides, state what its two operands are, and show the candidate satisfies it.
not_applicable_when: the deciding comparison has been identified and the candidate shown to satisfy it
no candidate has been adopted yet
misfire_risks: redundant once the deciding comparison is already pinned; the cost is one explicit statement of the evidence, not a blocked path
minimum_evidence_before_use: a candidate has been adopted
the comparison that decides acceptance has not been identified

retrieved_cards.title: Disassembly can desync and show a plausible-but-wrong instruction stream
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Instructions are being read at a fixed alignment where the real code overlaps, jumps into the middle of an instruction, or uses anti-disassembly, so the decoded stream may not be what executes.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A byte stream has multiple decodings; a linear or fixed-offset decode can lock onto the wrong one, producing instructions that look real but are not executed as shown.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Follow control flow into the region to fix the instruction boundaries, and re-disassemble at that alignment; where two decodings are possible, the one an incoming edge lands on is the one that runs.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The disassembly listing is the executed code, so I can reverse it as-is.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Verify the decode alignment against control flow; re-disassemble from the real entry points and follow the jumps to recover the instructions that actually run.
not_applicable_when: the disassembly alignment is confirmed by an incoming control-flow edge
the code region is known-clean with no overlap/anti-disasm
misfire_risks: most disassembly is correctly aligned; suspect desync specifically around indirect jumps, inline data, or obfuscated regions, not everywhere
minimum_evidence_before_use: a region shows overlap / jump-into-instruction / anti-disassembly characteristics
its alignment has not been confirmed against an incoming control-flow edge

retrieved_cards.title: Inline data or junk bytes can be rendered as instructions
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Bytes that are actually data (jump tables, constants, padding) or deliberate junk are being decoded and read as executable instructions.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: The boundary between code and data is ambiguous to the tool; non-code bytes decoded as instructions create spurious logic that never executes.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Check how the region is referenced (branched to, vs loaded as data) and whether any control-flow edge reaches it; a region with only data references is not code.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: These decoded instructions are real code, so they participate in the logic.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Confirm a control-flow edge reaches the region as code, rather than it being referenced as data, before reversing it.
not_applicable_when: the region is confirmed to be the target of a control-flow edge
the bytes are clearly referenced as data
misfire_risks: genuine code can look data-like; base the call on references and reachability, not on the bytes looking unusual
minimum_evidence_before_use: a region decoded as instructions has data-like or junk characteristics
no control-flow edge into it has been identified

The function fcn.00401861 is an interpreter/dispatcher. It reads a program counter from [0x63bb08] and uses that as an index into a jump table at [0x404170]. The value 19 (0x13) at 0x404080 is the modulus - when the index mod 19 = 18, the loop exits. Otherwise, index mod 19 selects one of 18 functions from the table at 0x4040e0.

The target bytes for comparison are at 0x4040a0: d1d0 62c7 a4a0 a333 5c36 caf0 9e57 6525 10db a538 db1a f135 467d c2ba 89d6 26a5 e198 1712 2215 1a03 0801 7bdd ee50 7cbb 5ef2 cb8b d464 0c23 b4a8 4093 ae81 2e28

I need to analyze each opcode function to understand the transformation and reverse it to find the 64-character input.

# Let's extract the bytecode and analyze the functions
# First, read the bytecode from 0x404180

import struct

# Read target binary
with open("/work/target", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()

# Find offsets for relevant data structures
# ELF base address to file offset conversion
# The binary is an ELF with the sections at specific addresses

# Read ELF headers to find sections
elf_header = data[:64]
e_phoff = struct.unpack_from("<Q", data, 32)[0]
e_phnum = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, 56)[0]
e_phentsize = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, 54)[0]

# Map virtual addresses to file offsets
def va_to_file_offset(va):
    for i in range(e_phnum):
        ph_offset = e_phoff + i * e_phentsize
        ph = data[ph_offset:ph_offset+e_phentsize]
        p_type = struct.unpack_from("<I", ph, 0)[0]
        if p_type != 1:  # PT_LOAD
            continue
        p_offset = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 8)[0]
        p_vaddr = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 16)[0]
        p_filesz = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 32)[0]
        p_memsz = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 40)[0]
        if p_vaddr <= va < p_vaddr + p_filesz:
            return p_offset + (va - p_vaddr)
    return None

# Read the jump table entries from 0x4040e0
func_table_va = 0x4040e0
func_table_file_offset = va_to_file_offset(func_table_va)
print(f"Function table at file offset: {func_table_file_offset}")

# Read 18 function pointers (18 * 8 bytes)
func_ptrs = []
for i in range(18):
    offset = func_table_file_offset + i * 8
    ptr = struct.unpack_from("<Q", data, offset)[0]
    func_ptrs.append(ptr)
    print(f"Function {i}: 0x{ptr:08x}")

# Read the bytecode from 0x404180
bytecode_va = 0x404180
bytecode_file_offset = va_to_file_offset(bytecode_va)
print(f"\nBytecode at file offset: {bytecode_file_offset}")

# Read bytecode (enough to analyze)
bytecode_data = data[bytecode_file_offset:bytecode_file_offset+1024]
print("Bytecode first 128 bytes:")
print(bytecode_data[:128].hex())

# Interpret the bytecode - each 8-byte entry mod 19
print("\nBytecode opcodes (mod 19):")
for i in range(0, 128, 8):
    val = struct.unpack_from("<Q", bytecode_data, i)[0]
    opcode = val % 19
    print(f"  [{i//8}]: 0x{val:016x} -> opcode {opcode}")

retrieved_cards.mechanism: A byte stream has multiple decodings; a linear or fixed-offset decode can lock onto the wrong one, producing instructions that look real but are not executed as shown.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Follow control flow into the region to fix the instruction boundaries, and re-disassemble at that alignment; where two decodings are possible, the one an incoming edge lands on is the one that runs.

retrieved_cards.title: Disassembly can desync and show a plausible-but-wrong instruction stream
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Instructions are being read at a fixed alignment where the real code overlaps, jumps into the middle of an instruction, or uses anti-disassembly, so the decoded stream may not be what executes.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A byte stream has multiple decodings; a linear or fixed-offset decode can lock onto the wrong one, producing instructions that look real but are not executed as shown.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Follow control flow into the region to fix the instruction boundaries, and re-disassemble at that alignment; where two decodings are possible, the one an incoming edge lands on is the one that runs.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The disassembly listing is the executed code, so I can reverse it as-is.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Verify the decode alignment against control flow; re-disassemble from the real entry points and follow the jumps to recover the instructions that actually run.
not_applicable_when: the disassembly alignment is confirmed by an incoming control-flow edge
the code region is known-clean with no overlap/anti-disasm
misfire_risks: most disassembly is correctly aligned; suspect desync specifically around indirect jumps, inline data, or obfuscated regions, not everywhere
minimum_evidence_before_use: a region shows overlap / jump-into-instruction / anti-disassembly characteristics
its alignment has not been confirmed against an incoming control-flow edge

retrieved_cards.validation_note: Check how the region is referenced (branched to, vs loaded as data) and whether any control-flow edge reaches it; a region with only data references is not code.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: These decoded instructions are real code, so they participate in the logic.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Confirm a control-flow edge reaches the region as code, rather than it being referenced as data, before reversing it.

the bytes are clearly referenced as data

retrieved_cards.title: A candidate never traced to a decision that would accept it
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A candidate has been adopted, but no comparison in the binary has been identified whose outcome on that candidate selects the accepting branch; the analysis proceeds as though it had passed.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Absence of an observed contradiction is conflated with positive support. With no execution available a candidate carries no acceptance evidence at all until it is traced to the comparison that decides.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Name the deciding comparison and both of its operands. If either operand cannot be pinned to a concrete value, the candidate is unsupported rather than confirmed -- that is a different state from being wrong, and it should be said explicitly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Nothing in the analysis contradicted this candidate, so it is the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Acceptance has to be positively derived: name the comparison that decides, state what its two operands are, and show the candidate satisfies it.
not_applicable_when: the deciding comparison has been identified and the candidate shown to satisfy it
no candidate has been adopted yet
misfire_risks: redundant once the deciding comparison is already pinned; the cost is one explicit statement of the evidence, not a blocked path

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path
the XOR is applied to an unrelated buffer, not the input being checked
misfire_risks: the key may be position-dependent / rolling rather than a single constant byte; assuming a single-byte key yields a wrong pre-image -- verify the key schedule before inverting
minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract XOR-then-compare; no task-specific keys, constants, or symbols.

retrieved_cards.title: Compared against a one-way digest: do NOT try to invert it
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The input is compared against a fixed-length, high-entropy constant produced by a one-way function (hash/checksum); the transform is not reversible.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Unlike invertible encodings, a digest cannot be reversed to the input; the visible digest is the comparison target, submitting it raw fails, and inverting it is also futile.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Identify the function as one-way; redirect effort to finding or constraining the pre-image rather than inverting; confirm a candidate by computing the digest of the candidate yourself and checking it equals the compared constant.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Submit the digest, or attempt to 'decrypt'/invert the hash to recover the input.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Recognize a one-way function: the accepted input must be found another way (located in the binary/inputs, or recovered by a constrained search), not by inverting the digest.
not_applicable_when: the transform is actually reversible (XOR/shift/encoding -- use the matching card and invert)
the constant is not a digest of the input
misfire_risks: mislabeling a reversible transform as one-way stops a valid inversion; distinguish a true digest (fixed length, avalanche) from an invertible encoding before abandoning inversion
minimum_evidence_before_use: the comparison target is a fixed-length high-entropy constant
the producing function matches a known one-way construction

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract one-way-digest counter-case; no task-specific hashes or constants.

    e_phentsize = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, 54)[0]

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path
the XOR is applied to an unrelated buffer, not the input being checked
misfire_risks: the key may be position-dependent / rolling rather than a single constant byte; assuming a single-byte key yields a wrong pre-image -- verify the key schedule before inverting
minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract XOR-then-compare; no task-specific keys, constants, or symbols.

retrieved_cards.title: A compared constant is the post-transform target, not the accepted input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The accept check compares a constant (often in .rodata) against the input only after the input passes through a transform (arithmetic, bitwise, or encoding); the constant is the value the transformed input must equal.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A constant on the comparison path is read as the answer, but the comparison is against transform(input); the accepted input is the pre-image, not the constant.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Trace the transform on the input path and identify what must be inverted; then re-apply the transform to the recovered pre-image and check it reproduces the compared constant exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The visible constant is the flag and can be submitted directly.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: The constant is the post-transform comparison target; the accepted input is whatever transforms into it. Recover the pre-image before submitting.
not_applicable_when: the comparison is against the raw input with no transform on the path (then the constant may be the answer)
the constant is confirmed to be the operand compared against the raw input, with the transform applied elsewhere
the constant is used for output/formatting, not in the accept comparison
misfire_risks: may cause a constant to be dismissed even in trivial checks where the input is compared raw; confirm a transform is actually present before discarding the constant
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant is observed on the comparison path
a transform is observed between the input and the comparison

I can now understand the VM execution flow better. Each opcode function throws an exception after doing its work, and the exception handler at 0x4018d7-0x4018eb catches it and increments the PC by rbx. The key insight is that after each operation, the function throws "BAAAAM" exception, and the handler adds rbx (a register set during the function) to the PC counter at 0x63bb08.

Looking at opcode functions:
- Opcode 0 (0x4011d6): Loads bytecode[pc+1] into a stack slot at [rsp - 0x1000]
- Opcode 1 (0x40123a): Just throws (nop)
- Opcode 2 (0x401283): ADD - adds [rsp-0xff0] to [rsp-0xfe0]
- Opcode 3 (0x4012dc): SUB - subtracts [rsp-0xff0] from [rsp-0xfe0]
- Opcode 4 (0x401335): MUL - multiplies
- Opcode 5 (0x401396): AND - bitwise AND
- Opcode 6 (0x401448): OR - bitwise OR
- Opcode 7 (0x4013ef): XOR - bitwise XOR
- Opcode 8 (0x4014a1): SHL - shift left
- Opcode 9 (0x401509): SHR - shift right
- Opcode 10 (0x401571): Copies [rsp-0xff0] to [rsp-0x1000] (push dup)
- Opcode 11 (0x4015ca): SWAP [rsp-0xff0] and [rsp-0xfe0]
- Opcode 12 (0x40162b): Loads stack[bytecode[pc+1]*2] to [rsp-0x1000]
- Opcode 13 (0x40169f): Loads input[stack[-1]] to stack[-1]
- Opcode 14 (0x401700): Stores stack[-1] to input[stack[-2]]
- Opcode 15 (0x401761): Compare equal - sets stack[-1] = (stack[-1] == stack[-2])
- Opcode 16 (0x4017cf): Just throws (nop)
- Opcode 17 (0x401818): Just throws (nop)
- Opcode 18: EXIT

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path
the XOR is applied to an unrelated buffer, not the input being checked
misfire_risks: the key may be position-dependent / rolling rather than a single constant byte; assuming a single-byte key yields a wrong pre-image -- verify the key schedule before inverting
minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

retrieved_cards.title: A compared constant is the post-transform target, not the accepted input

retrieved_cards.mechanism: A constant on the comparison path is read as the answer, but the comparison is against transform(input); the accepted input is the pre-image, not the constant.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Trace the transform on the input path and identify what must be inverted; then re-apply the transform to the recovered pre-image and check it reproduces the compared constant exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The visible constant is the flag and can be submitted directly.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: The constant is the post-transform comparison target; the accepted input is whatever transforms into it. Recover the pre-image before submitting.

minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant is observed on the comparison path
a transform is observed between the input and the comparison

retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The accept check compares a constant (often in .rodata) against the input only after the input passes through a transform (arithmetic, bitwise, or encoding); the constant is the value the transformed input must equal.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A constant on the comparison path is read as the answer, but the comparison is against transform(input); the accepted input is the pre-image, not the constant.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Trace the transform on the input path and identify what must be inverted; then re-apply the transform to the recovered pre-image and check it reproduces the compared constant exactly.

# Now let me extract all the PC increments from DWARF unwind info and simulate the VM

import subprocess
import struct
import re

with open("/work/target", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()

def va_to_file_offset(va):
    e_phoff = struct.unpack_from("<Q", data, 32)[0]
    e_phnum = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, 56)[0]
    e_phentsize = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, 54)[0]
    for i in range(e_phnum):
        ph_offset = e_phoff + i * e_phentsize
        ph = data[ph_offset:ph_offset+e_phentsize]
        p_type = struct.unpack_from("<I", ph, 0)[0]
        if p_type != 1:
            continue
        p_offset = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 8)[0]
        p_vaddr = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 16)[0]
        p_filesz = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 32)[0]
        if p_vaddr <= va < p_vaddr + p_filesz:
            return p_offset + (va - p_vaddr)
    return None

# Get all DWARF unwind info
result = subprocess.run(['readelf', '-wf', '/work/target'], capture_output=True, text=True)
dwarf_output = result.stdout

# Parse the FDE entries to get rbx values for each function
# Function addresses to opcode mapping:
func_addrs = [0x4011d6, 0x40123a, 0x401283, 0x4012dc, 0x401335, 0x401396, 
              0x401448, 0x4013ef, 0x4014a1, 0x401509, 0x401571, 0x4015ca,
              0x40162b, 0x40169f, 0x401700, 0x401761, 0x4017cf, 0x401818]

# Parse from the output - looking for patterns like:
# FDE ... pc=START..END
# DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: N)

# Let me extract manually based on what I saw:
# Opcode 0 (0x4011d6): rbx = 2
# Opcode 1 (0x40123a): rbx = 1
# Opcode 2 (0x401283): rbx = 1
# ... need to get all of them

# Let me find all entries
fde_pattern = r'FDE.*pc=([0-9a-f]+)\.\.([0-9a-f]+)'
rbx_pattern = r'DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 \(rbx\) \(DW_OP_constu: (\d+)\)'

fde_entries = []
lines = dwarf_output.split('\n')
current_fde = None
for line in lines:
    fde_match = re.search(fde_pattern, line)
    if fde_match:
        current_fde = {'start': int(fde_match.group(1), 16), 'end': int(fde_match.group(2), 16)}
    rbx_match = re.search(rbx_pattern, line)
    if rbx_match and current_fde:
        current_fde['rbx'] = int(rbx_match.group(1))
        fde_entries.append(current_fde)
        current_fde = None

# Map function address to rbx value
opcode_pc_inc = {}
for entry in fde_entries:
    start = entry['start']
    rbx = entry['rbx']
    if start in func_addrs:
        idx = func_addrs.index(start)
        opcode_pc_inc[idx] = rbx
        print(f"Opcode {idx} (0x{start:08x}): PC += {rbx}")

print(f"\nTotal opcodes with PC increments: {len(opcode_pc_inc)}")

# Now let me simulate the VM and trace the operations
import struct

with open("/work/target", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()

def va_to_file_offset(va):
    e_phoff = struct.unpack_from("<Q", data, 32)[0]
    e_phnum = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, 56)[0]
    e_phentsize = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, 54)[0]
    for i in range(e_phnum):
        ph_offset = e_phoff + i * e_phentsize
        ph = data[ph_offset:ph_offset+e_phentsize]
        p_type = struct.unpack_from("<I", ph, 0)[0]
        if p_type != 1:
            continue
        p_offset = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 8)[0]
        p_vaddr = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 16)[0]
        p_filesz = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 32)[0]
        if p_vaddr <= va < p_vaddr + p_filesz:
            return p_offset + (va - p_vaddr)
    return None

# Read bytecode
bytecode_va = 0x404180
bytecode_file_offset = va_to_file_offset(bytecode_va)
bytecode_data = data[bytecode_file_offset:bytecode_file_offset+4096]
bytecode = [struct.unpack_from("<Q", bytecode_data, i*8)[0] for i in range(300)]

# PC increments per opcode
pc_inc = {
    0: 2, 1: 1, 2: 1, 3: 1, 4: 1, 5: 1, 6: 1, 7: 1,
    8: 1, 9: 1, 10: 1, 11: 1, 12: 2, 13: 1, 14: 1, 15: 1, 16: 1, 17: 1
}

# Opcode names
opcode_names = {
    0: "PUSH_IMM", 1: "NOP1", 2: "ADD", 3: "SUB", 4: "MUL", 5: "AND",
    6: "OR", 7: "XOR", 8: "SHL", 9: "SHR", 10: "DUP?", 11: "SWAP",
    12: "DUP_IDX", 13: "LOAD_INPUT", 14: "STORE_INPUT", 15: "CMP_EQ",
    16: "NOP16", 17: "NOP17", 18: "EXIT"
}

# Simulate execution
class VM:
    def __init__(self, input_vals):
        self.input = list(input_vals)  # 8 x uint64
        self.stack = []  # List of values
        self.pc = 0
        
    def run(self, trace=False):
        while True:
            opcode = bytecode[self.pc] % 19
            if opcode == 18:
                if trace:
                    print(f"PC={self.pc}: EXIT")
                break
                
            if trace:
                imm = bytecode[self.pc + 1] if pc_inc.get(opcode, 1) == 2 else None
                print(f"PC={self.pc}: {opcode_names.get(opcode, f'OP{opcode}')} {'0x'+format(imm,'x') if imm else ''} | stack={[hex(x) for x in self.stack[-3:]]}")
            
            self.execute(opcode)
            self.pc += pc_inc.get(opcode, 1)
        return self.input
    
    def execute(self, opcode):
        if opcode == 0:  # PUSH immediate
            imm = bytecode[self.pc + 1]
            self.stack.append(imm)
        elif opcode == 1:  # NOP
            pass

# Now I understand the VM better. Let me re-implement with correct opcode 16 and 17 handling
import struct

with open("/work/target", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()

def va_to_file_offset(va):
    e_phoff = struct.unpack_from("<Q", data, 32)[0]
    e_phnum = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, 56)[0]
    e_phentsize = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, 54)[0]
    for i in range(e_phnum):
        ph_offset = e_phoff + i * e_phentsize
        ph = data[ph_offset:ph_offset+e_phentsize]
        p_type = struct.unpack_from("<I", ph, 0)[0]
        if p_type != 1:
            continue
        p_offset = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 8)[0]
        p_vaddr = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 16)[0]
        p_filesz = struct.unpack_from("<Q", ph, 32)[0]
        if p_vaddr <= va < p_vaddr + p_filesz:
            return p_offset + (va - p_vaddr)
    return None

# Read bytecode
bytecode_va = 0x404180
bytecode_file_offset = va_to_file_offset(bytecode_va)
bytecode_data = data[bytecode_file_offset:bytecode_file_offset+4096]
bytecode = [struct.unpack_from("<Q", bytecode_data, i*8)[0] for i in range(300)]

# Read target values
target_va = 0x4040a0
target_file_offset = va_to_file_offset(target_va)
target_bytes = data[target_file_offset:target_file_offset+64]
target_values = [struct.unpack_from("<Q", target_bytes, i*8)[0] for i in range(8)]

# Opcode names
opcode_names = {
    0: "PUSH_IMM", 1: "NOP", 2: "ADD", 3: "SUB", 4: "MUL", 5: "AND",
    6: "OR", 7: "XOR", 8: "SHL", 9: "SHR", 10: "DUP", 11: "SWAP",
    12: "DUP_IDX", 13: "LOAD_INPUT", 14: "STORE_INPUT", 15: "CMP_EQ",
    16: "JMP", 17: "JZ", 18: "EXIT"
}

class VM:
    def __init__(self, input_vals):
        self.input = list(input_vals)  # 8 x uint64
        self.stack = []
        self.pc = 0
        
    def run(self, trace=False, max_steps=1000):
        steps = 0
        while steps < max_steps:
            opcode = bytecode[self.pc] % 19
            if opcode == 18:
                if trace:
                    print(f"PC={self.pc}: EXIT")
                break
                
            if trace:
                stack_str = [hex(x) for x in self.stack[-5:]] if len(self.stack) > 0 else []
                print(f"PC={self.pc}: {opcode_names.get(opcode, f'OP{opcode}')} | stack_len={len(self.stack)} top={stack_str}")
            
            pc_delta = self.execute(opcode)
            self.pc += pc_delta
            steps += 1
            
        return self.input
    
    def execute(self, opcode):
        if opcode == 0:  # PUSH immediate
            imm = bytecode[self.pc + 1]
            self.stack.append(imm)
            return 2
        elif opcode == 1:  # NOP
            return 1
        elif opcode == 2:  # ADD
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append((a + b) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 3:  # SUB
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append((a - b) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 4:  # MUL
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append((a * b) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 5:  # AND
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(a & b)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 6:  # OR
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(a | b)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 7:  # XOR
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(a ^ b)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 8:  # SHL
            b = self.stack.pop() & 63
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append((a << b) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 9:  # SHR
            b = self.stack.pop() & 63
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(a >> b)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 10:  # DUP top
            self.stack.append(self.stack[-1])
            return 1
        elif opcode == 11:  # SWAP
            a = self.stack.pop()
            b = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(a)
            self.stack.append(b)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 12:  # DUP indexed
            idx = bytecode[self.pc + 1]
            val = self.stack[-(idx + 1)]
            self.stack.append(val)
            return 2
        elif opcode == 13:  # LOAD input[idx]
            idx = self.stack.pop()
            if idx < 8:
                self.stack.append(self.input[idx])
            else:
                self.stack.append(0)  # Out of bounds
            return 1
        elif opcode == 14:  # STORE input[idx]
            val = self.stack.pop()
            idx = self.stack.pop()
            if idx < 8:
                self.input[idx] = val
            return 1
        elif opcode == 15:  # CMP EQ
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(1 if a == b else 0)
            return 1
        elif opcode == 16:  # JMP (unconditional)
            # PC += stack[-1]
            offset = self.stack.pop()
            return offset
        elif opcode == 17:  # JZ (conditional jump)
            # if stack[-2] == 0: PC += stack[-1] else PC += 1
            offset = self.stack.pop()
            cond = self.stack.pop()
            if cond == 0:
                return offset
            else:
                return 1
        return 1

# Test with dummy input
test_input = [0x4141414141414141] * 8
vm = VM(test_input)
result = vm.run(trace=True, max_steps=200)
